title: Bill C-39, Bill C-22 and Quebec's Bill 21: What you need to know

blocks.text: Politics·New

In Parliament, a bill is a written proposal for a new piece of Canadian law. Those proposals make the news because they're typically about big-ticket issues that affect Canadians across the entire country, like everyday affordability or personal privacy. Here's what to know about those in the headlines this month.
From major infrastructure to online privacy, federal bills have been up for debate in November
Almost daily, bills make the news across Canada. Stories are often about the bills you have to pay on a regular basis, but November has brought plenty of updates about the bills that can become law.

In Parliament, a bill is a written proposal for a new piece of Canadian law or changes to an existing law. Those proposals make the news because they're typically about big-ticket issues that affect Canadians across the country, like everyday affordability or personal privacy.
Here's a breakdown of those in the headlines this month.
Bill C-39
Carney's major projects bill faces growing environmental, labour pushback

Bill C-39 is also known as the Building Canada Strong Act. It's a controversial piece of legislation designed to give the federal government the power to fast-track the approval process for major projects in regions deemed to be in the national interest.
Major projects could be mines, pipelines, power lines and other infrastructure.

The bill has been the subject of debate because it contains more than 300 clauses amending more than a dozen existing pieces of federal legislation, including laws to protect species at risk, water quality and fisheries. The bill also includes proposed changes to the Canada Labour Code, which left unions unimpressed.

The special legislative committee voted to approve the bill with some amendments on Monday, bringing a days-long, clause-by-clause debate to an end. The bill is expected to be debated in the House of Commons again soon and could become law before the holiday break in December.
Bill C-22
Liberals propose new police search powers bill after privacy concerns thwarted 1st attempt
Known as lawful access legislation, Bill C-22 is a deeply divisive legislative proposal that would make it easier for police and intelligence agencies to access Canadians' private information.

If the bill becomes law, tech companies would be compelled to adapt their systems to preserve data and then turn that information over to law enforcement and the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS) if either had a warrant.

The bill would also give the federal public safety minister the power to issue confidential orders requiring electronic service providers to retain user metadata, which can include the sender, recipient and timing of communications, for as long as six months.

The government and security community argue the bill is essential for investigators to keep pace in a digital age. Privacy proponents, civil liberties groups and some of the world's largest tech companies, on the other hand, have raised concerned about opening up access to encrypted information.
This week, senators on the national security committee said they wanted to see some changes to the bill after another clause-by-clause review.
Bill 21
Why all Canadians’ rights are at stake in the Supreme Court challenge of Quebec’s Bill 21

This is Quebec's controversial secularism law, which bars some public-sector workers from wearing religious symbols on the job. The law, which applies to teachers and police officers, among others, quickly faced a constitutional challenge from civil liberties groups arguing that it discriminates against Muslim women who wear head coverings.
The law is technically no longer a bill because it was adopted by the Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) government in 2019, but has been commonly referred to as Bill 21 in media coverage for years.
That convention will continue when the Supreme Court of Canada issues its decision about the legislation Friday morning.
